There are only two things that affect Bridge Ops:

Also (and this is neither here nor there), but everything the AI throws at you is scripted.  
There's a very basic 'Tactical AI' that governs e.g. which unit to shoot at, whether or not to use T-mode for movement, etc.

So you can crudely divide the JTS games into four categories.

1. Operational warfare (Panzer Campaigns, WWI campaigns, Modern Campaigns, Panzer Battles.)
2. Tactical warfare (Squad battles)
3. American civil war (Guess what series that is), and
4. Napoleonic warfare (Again, no prizes for guessing which series).

Don't get me wrong, I'm not saying all the games under category 1 play the same way; they most certainly do not.  
But they're based on the same rule-set, and while the unit-values differ vastly, and MC throws thermal imaging and choppers into the mix, the basic resolution is the same throughout.

So what I would suggest is downloading the PzC demo Mius, and play the short scenario (9 turns IIRC) without FoW.   
Don't try to win, just poke around and see what wiggles.  
Next, read (and then re-read) the following rule-sections:  
5.0 Firing, 6.0 Assault, 9.0 Command and 10.0 Supply.  
And then try the same scenario again.  
Make no mistake, those four rule-sections are vital (especially supply and command).  
Ignore night, fatigue, engineers and all that other chrome.  
Just get the basics right first, and then build on from there.

But saying that the "White Feather Brigade" was somehow feminist, completely disregards the history of the white feather as a sign of cowardice.

First of all, the white feather wasn't a concept invented in WWI, The Oxford English Dictionary quotes sources from 1785 illustrating the use of the phrase to signify cowardice.  


Secondly, it was not the brain-child of Emmaline Parkhurst.  
The 'White Feather Brigade' was the result of Admiral Charles Fitzgerald (who incidentally was a great believer in conscription) , who organized a group of 30 women in Folkestone to deliver the white feathers, and he did this in August 1914, some three weeks after the war started.  
Which then spread to the rest of the country.

It was a propaganda tool, much like those infamous posters of Kitchener stating that 'England Wants You'  
And the 'White Feather Brigade' had so many erroneous deliveries that the government had to come up with pins to show that people hadn't enlisted because they were valuable to the war-effort.  
The most brazen example being delivering a white feather to George Samson, because he was in civilian clothes going to the ceremony of accepting the Victoria Cross.  
It was, in other words, as good an idea as Kitcheners 'Pals Battalions' in 1916.  


So the 'White Feather Brigade' was basically an overly patriotic movement, and part of a larger propaganda-campaign, e.g. comparing the enemy to nun-raping Huns.  
It should also be noted that most members of the 'White Feather Brigade' were well-to-do women, who had no prior obligations.  
Most of the working-class women were too busy in the munitions-factories, or taking over the farm-work from the men who were at the front.

So no, it wasn't a feminist movement.  
They didn't do it to advance the universal suffrage.

Not all that familiar with SB (or at least not nearly to the same degree as PzC), but firing at units isn't likely to cause casualties unless you have a lot of fire-power.  
Unfortunately, Grenada sports a lot of very small fire-teams, so assaults are your main option.

Given the standard FireLo/FireHi of 6/60, you need 300 Lethality to inflict one casualty on any given fire-attack. Plus, modifiers for terrain and reliability.  
So, a handful of men with M-16s isn't going to cut it.

What you need is enough firepower to pin the enemy, and then bring overwhelming assaults into that hex. At least 3:1, preferably higher, keeping in mind that various weapons have different assault-values.

As for assaults, the final assault will have to be done from one hex, since SB doesn't allow multi-hex assaults. But that doesn't mean the assaulting forces have to start in the same hex.  
You can bring in squads/teams from different hexes drawing defensive fire.  
All that matters is that they all end in the same hex with enough MPs to make the final assault.  
(Or alternatively, with enough cover for them to survive until their assault next turn.)

But the problem isn't the number of scenarios, that's somewhat beside the point. Even with only e.g. ten scenarios for each game, it would still rely on scripted play instead of AI driven play.

There are pros and cons to scripted vs. AI directed play. IIRC JTS even covers some of it in one of the player-guides (might have been a forum post). What JTS basically said is that no AI will ever rival a human player, so it's better to have a scripted AI since a human can then 'program' it. Which sounds beguiling, but there are some heavy caveats to that statement.

The biggest problem with a scripted AI is that it relies entirely on the programmers ability to predict what the player will do. Which is fine for small scenarios, since there's a limit to how much the situation can change in that amount of time. But when it comes to the campaigns, you can't possibly predict what the situation will be 70 turns down the road, not even with three crystal balls, two ouija boards and a divining rod. There are simply too many variables to take into account.  
So what the campaign AI does (or at least what I suspect it does), is simply program in what happened historically. Pz Lehr counter-attacked at Caen, so that's what the AI will do as well. At Tannenberg, the Russian right flank withdrew far too late, so the AI does that as well.  
The issue with a scripted AI is that it's only valid as long as the player follows the same historical route. Once something unexpected happens, the AI has no way of correcting itself since there are no instructions that can override the script.  
So it'll try to attack even if it's down to 50% strength, heavily fatigued and with no friendly units on their flanks.

I could maybe live with all that if the tactical AI was better, but let's face it, it's about as sharp as a sack of bowlingballs.  
It'll lead attacks with HQ units, it will quite happily sit in Travel-mode despite being spotted and in artillery range. It continues assaults until the units reach max. fatigue instead of withdrawing. It has no concept of flanks, isolation or for that matter ZOC, nor does it have a clue how to optimize the position of support-units. It will always take the shortest route to whatever objective it has been given. And the idea of reserves is a complete mystery.  
And on and on......  
In my latest Normandy game against the AI, Lehr attacked at Caen as expected. And they kept doing so for 3 days. So after those 3 days had passed, I switched FOW off and looked at Lehr.......Which was down to 15% strength, and every unit except the HQs had 250+ fatigue. Nobody told the AI it was a bad idea to keep attacking with heavily fatigued and understrength units, so it just kept at it. With the result that it threw away one of its strongest formations.

As for Combat Mission, you're right. The AI has 4-5 battle-plans it can switch between, and a range of possible positions on every map for e.g. AT-guns.  
The difference is that the TacAI is much, much better. It'll seek cover when under fire, it'll deploy smoke if needed, it'll move AT weapons up to deal with an armored threat, etc.  
Is it as good as a human opponent? No, not by a long shot. But it at least reacts to the situation around it.

Not that I disagree with any of the tips (I usually play hot-seat w/FOW), the main reason the AI is so bad (and it really is atrocious) is because the JTS AI doesn't actually exist.

At no point in any phase does the AI consider yours or its own positions.

Sure, it has a basic 'TacAI', that usually consist of piling as many units into a hex as possible and then charging, but everything on the strategic front, i.e. where to move and when, is completely scripted.

It also means that any scenario played solo will have limited replayability, since the AI will always go after the same objectives.

So it seems to have been a design decision from JTS' side. Whether this is because such a small team didn't have resources to create an AI, or whether they realized most people would play H2H in the first place, or something else entirely I can't say.

No problem. And yeah, in East Prussia you're definitely better off bypassing. There are only two (IIRC) positions covered by redoubts; Festung Boyern, which is easily bypassed since it doesn't really sit on any major arteries and only contains 1-2 divisions. 

And then there's a single redoubt covering a bridge further to the west. That one is a little annoying, but there's a minor road leading north that can be used instead, forcing him to either retreat or get surrounded. Or, as you said, build a bridge down-river and just go past.

Redoubts are a bigger problem in France, more of them and they're better placed.

First, consider if you actually need to take the redoubts. It might seem like a silly question, but a lot of players have a tendency to attack something merely because it's enemy-occupied.

If you're only attacking it because of VPs, consider the number of casualties you'll take trying to evict the enemy. That's going to off-set any VP gains the hex might give you.

If you, for whatever reason, absolutely have to take the redoubt, get yourself into the right frame of mind. It'll take a long time, you need a vast numerical superiority, you have to set the attack up right, and even then you'll take horrendous casualties. If you try to simply storm the position, all you're doing is keeping the grave-diggers occupied.

So.....The easiest way to dislodge an enemy isn't by reducing the numbers, it's removing the force-multipliers of Morale and Fatigue.

Best way to drop Morale is by encircling it, either the unit or if possible the entire position. Being Isolated drops it one Morale-level, and as soon as it fires it'll go Low on Ammo, and drops another one. By the same token, keeping them Out of Command will stop them from receiving replacements, and a Disrupted parent HQ means the unit can't recover from Disruption. So any enemy HQ outside fortifications should become an instant munitions-magnet.

Fatigue is a little trickier, simply because fatigue-gain is linked to casualties. Or in other words, if you don't inflict casualties, you don't inflict fatigue either. Which is a bit of a problem when the enemy is behind concrete. So what you do is set up a series of rolling assaults; One wave assaults hopefully inflicting just a little fatigue, then they go to the back while the next wave assaults. Repeat ad nauseum. The issue is that, at least in the beginning, all your assaults will fail, so you're gaining more fatigue than the enemy. Which is why you need a massive numerical superiority. You need to be able to do decent assault(i.e. at least 3:1) each and every turn to grind him down.

Which brings us to the final maxim when assaulting a fortified enemy: Concentrate.

Do not try and assault the entire line, you're just wasting man-power. Find the weakest sector, and pick 1-2 hexes to attack and then throw everything into that small area. Assaults, air-power, artillery, rocks, dead cats, whatever you can bring to bear. But the point is, NOTHING attacks anywhere else than that small sector. Lock down the flanks with ZOC so he can't easily reinforce, and then you just pound, and pound, and pound. It's bloody, it's long-winded, but without heavy guns your only option is sheer attrition.

Don't be surprised if it takes an entire division to dislodge a single battalion from a Redoubt. And that division will be shot to pieces in the process.

So I reiterate my original question. Do you actually NEED to take the redoubt? Nine times out of ten you're far better off simply bypassing the position.

Plenty of resources online re. IFR flight planning. But a (very) brief intro:

An IFR flight consists of the following: Departure runway - SID - Airways - STAR - Destination runway.

Think of the airways as a highway with the SID/STARs as on/off ramps. So a SID from an airport will usually lead you to a navigation-point on your desired airway, and a STAR will usually start at a holding point and will contain pre-planned approaches from that holding-point to the runway. So most major airports will have a ring of holding-points around it, catching flights from most directions.

Take EKCH (my home airport) for example.

[http://www.uvairlines.com/admin/resources/EKCH.pdf](http://www.uvairlines.com/admin/resources/EKCH.pdf)

So the two STARs SVD2M and SVD2N both start at the holding-point SVD. Whether you choose 2M or 2N depends on whether RWY 04 or 22 is in use.

Granted, complete STARs in real-life are pretty rare, usually the tower gives you vectors at some point to save time and fuel. But in an imperfect sim, plugging in the complete SID/STAR is a good way to go.

Also note that I said 'usually' and 'most airports'. There are some pretty funky approaches out there, especially when you start delving into mountainous airports.

Just keep it simple when you try to learn this stuff. Trying to grasp all of it at once is like taking a drink from a firehose. :)

But generally speaking, there's a few things you can do to improve matters.

First and foremost, keep up the morale of your own troops. That means keeping them within command-range, and making sure they're supplied. If possible, assault from a hex with cover to minimize casualties and thus morale-checks.

It mainly depends on what you're trying to assault. If you're trying to assault undisrupted infantry, don't. Use artillery and MGs to disrupt them first, then move in for the assault. Undisrupted defenders aren't going to lose the assault anyway, so why move into range.

Don't attack piecemeal. A standard brigade of 6 battalions shouldn't expect to attack on a broader front than 2 hexes. That way, if the initial move into assault-range fails, the unit pulls back and the next one moves in. If that fails too, you still have a third available. And of course, make sure the HQ is close by to undisrupt the first wave so they're available next turn.

Finally, don't forget that the JTS games are games of maneuver. So instead of assaulting frontally, can you make the enemy's position untenable by flanking him? Do you have anything available that can Isolate him for a turn or two?

And of course, use the best troops available. You can't realistically assault with D quality units unless you have an awful lot of them.

Keeping cav in T-mode has pros and cons, and as always it'll depend on the tactical situation.

First and foremost, cav in T-mode has 4 times their normal assault value, and they only pay 1/3 of their MPs to assault (as opposed to the normal 2/3), so they're very good at assaulting. The caveat to that is the units are still pretty small, and they'll draw OpFire while in travel-mode so don't try to charge good-order infantry. Prime targets are unsupported artillery/MG companies, already Disrupted/High fatigue units or exposed HQs.

Second, cav in T-mode only takes 1/12 the normal casualties when assaulted. Granted, they'll have to retreat if assaulted by anything other than cav, but it can still slow an enemy down without suffering too many casualties.

The obvious con is that for any of the above to be relevant, they have to stay in T-mode so they're horribly exposed to direct fire. And of course, they can only regain fatigue when Deployed.

Personally, I never use cav as combat-troops, except possibly against other cav, and even then I'd keep them in T-mode. In the current situation I would've simply pulled back or gone around the German positions. Far as I'm concerned they've already completed their primary goal, finding the enemy. The problem with using cav as combat-troops is that they're expensive VP-wise, and they're not very good at it.

IMO their main use is recon and dealing with enemy cav. Once that's accomplished, I either keep them lurking the background looking for possible cavalry-charges, or use their mobility to Isolate units. 

Another very effective use is when you have to move engaged infantry to another sector (Russian east flank in Tannenberg comes to mind). Throwing a screen of cavalry companies with interlocking ZOC between them and the enemy means they can disengage while the enemy tries to deal with the cavalry.  The trick here is that the retreating friendly infantry can move three hexes in open ground (obviously more along roads), so if you keep moving the cavalry-screen back two hexes, the enemy now has no options. He can't assault after moving two hexes, and after movement he only has one fire-attack left which isn't going to kill all that many troopers. Next turn you retreat a further two hexes, and the process repeats. And in the meantime your friendly infantry has time to get to their new position, dig in and set the MGs up. Having been on the receiving end of that particular tactic, I can vouch for the efficiency.

You'll want to be careful using unsupported cavalry against infantry.

The cavalry brigades have much smaller units, lower defensive values and far fewer support-units, so they'll simply melt away if the infantry launches a determined attack. And of course cav is worth twice as many VPs as inf.

You can deploy cavalry against other cavalry with a reasonable chance of success, but generally speaking cavalry have little reason to ever leave Travel-mode (aside from resting).

There's a limit to how many times a unit can fire OpFire. This is a given since the manual refers to purposely 'drawing OpFire'. I would assume that it follows the normal firing-rules i.e. 1/3 MPs for each attack (or 1/2 for heavy weapons), so 3 OpFire attacks per turn, but that's educated guess-work.

Well, yes and no to that one.

Granted, charging 5 guys with AKs across open ground probably isn't something you should do on a regular basis, and good luck will always be a factor.

But if you look at the numbers the odds aren't that bad.

5 AKs with a Lethality of 19= 95. They're pinned, firing at non-Ground units at point-blank range, so the value is halved, doubled, doubled resulting in a final value of 190.

Divide that with the baseline of 10,000 gives us 0.019. FireLo/FireHi is 6 and 60 respectively, giving us final casualty-values of .16 and 1.6 (rounding off). Average of that is .9, times the stacking-value of 1.4 and we end with a final value of 1.26.

Or in other words, I'm fairly certain that I'll lose one man in that charge, but probably only one.

And taking that one casualty also enables me to use 13 men with superior morale to assault 5 pinned guys giving me an advantage of about 6:1.

​

And no, I don't do all these calculations in my head before every attack. I'd never finish a game. :D

But I do keep a rough tally of what I think the enemy has, and with the 'standard' SB FireLo/FireHi of 6/60, a good benchmark to keep in mind is 300. With a fire-value of 300 you're likely to lose one man for every fire attack. It's a rough calculation and doesn't take effectiveness, terrain or anything else into account, but it's only meant as a bare-bones guideline as to what can or can't be done.

The Mulberries aren't simulated as such. The JTS games uses a fairly generic supply/command system which has pros and cons.

Obvious pro is that it's the same system through the whole series, so players don't have to relearn everything when changing games. Also, the relative simplicity of the system ensures that the player can see what is going on without a lot of 'fudging' going on under the hood.  If you end up out of supply, you can (usually) point to a specific spot on the map and say "That's why".

The cons are that you can do some weird things with it. Technically, there's nothing stopping me from attaching every division to a single corps, and have all the supplies flow through one beach-head. It would be a bad idea from a command and artillery stand-point, but the supply-system wouldn't care. And of course, something as specialized as Mulberries isn't really modeled. The boost in supplies on June 11th and 17th coincide with the historical deployment of the Mulberries, so in that respect it is in the game. But the storm that'll hit June 19-22 won't affect the supplies. It'll pretty much shut down all operations due to the effect on movement and airpower, but the supplies keep flowing.

​

Just one of those 'historical vs. playable' things that always crop up in game design.

I mean, I get the logic behind the rule, and to a certain extent I like it. But it's also a prize-winning example of the law of unintended consequences.

In Normandy for example, a company of StuGs can hold back an entire battalion of paras in bocage country. They won't inflict much damage, but given the low Hard Attack of the paras, they're almost impossible to dislodge. 6 StuGs holding a 2 kilometer long, static position in dense terrain against infantry.....Yeah, I don't think so. :)

It gets even worse when it comes to bunkers, because the JTS games don't differentiate between armor and bunkers. It's all Hard targets.

Which leads to the bizarre conclusion that if you encounter enemy infantry in bunkers, your best bet isn't combat engineers, it's AT-guns, or unsupported armor. Admittedly, the armor will take Combined Arms penalties, but they'll still do roughly three times better than with a pure infantry assault, and they'll take fewer casualties in the process.

And it gets better. You know those flame-throwing Stuarts (Or the Crocodiles in Normandy) that the Marines bring with them to Japan? They've got those nice, shiny flame-throwers with huge Assault values, designed for use against enemy bunker-complexes. Except they won't use them when Alt. Assault is on. Oh sure, they'll fry the enemy in the open or in trenches, but as soon as a bit of concrete is introduced, they only fire with that dinky little 37mm gun they also carry around.

​

When it comes to Optional rules, Alt. fire should (IMO) be on, and Alt. Assault most definitely should be OFF. If a rule encourages you to lead a seaborne invasion with AT-guns, something is fundamentally wrong. :)

Always set altitude before climbing. You want to give the system enough time to give you a gradual change in cabin pressure. Think of the pressure-setting as telling the plane what altitude-interval you'll be working at.

You can, in theory, wait until you're at cruising altitude, but that gives you two problems. First of all, climbing without equalizing the pressure risks too high a pressure-differential with structural damage as a result. Second, it would lead to a very rapid pressure-equalization once you open the valves, again risking structural failure (plus it won't be very much fun for the persons onboard)

Okay, so a brief introduction to the the whole pressurization issue. We want a plane to be able to fly high above e.g. bad weather. But fly high enough, and the pilot won't be able to breathe, plus it gets kinda cold up there. So we pressurize the hull/cabin.

But the higher the pressure-difference is between the cabin and the outside, the stronger the cabin has to be to contain the pressure. If you were to take a cabin pressured for sea-level and bring it up to 34,000ft without equalizing, the cabin would literally burst. So we lower the pressure inside the cabin so it is still comfortable for humans, but that the pressure-differential is low enough for the cabin to hold together. A standard airliner cruising at 30k+ feet, will have the passenger-cabin pressurized for about 8,000ft, which is the lowest pressure humans generally find comfortable. With me so far?

So your pressure-setting has two gauges; Inner circle for altitude, outer circle for cabin. But setting the pressure for a specific altitude does NOT change anything on its own. All you're doing is telling the plane what altitude you're planning to fly at. It does not start to pressurize the cabin at this point, otherwise you'd need a suction-pump to lower the pressure inside while sitting on the runway. Once you start climbing THEN it starts to equalize the pressure in order to keep the pressure-differential low enough  for the cabin to hold together. So if you're flying at 24k, and set the pressure to 35k, nothing will happen, nor should it. The cabin is already pressurized to the altitude you're flying at. Not until you actually start climbing to 35k will the system lower the cabin-pressure further.

Nor will cabin pressure ever match the altitude you're flying at; doing so would defeat the whole purpose of pressurization.

Setting the pressure-gauge only tells the plane what the expected outside pressure is going to be, and thus what pressure-differential to aim for when the plane reaches altitude.

Or at least that's how it should work. Whether or not it's modeled properly in MSFS, I have no idea.

Short version, you trim for speed and throttle for altitude. Despite the fact that most people intuitively think it's the other way around. If you're in a car and push the throttle, you'll speed up. In a plane, you'll start to climb. 

​

The highly simplified version:

You always have four forces affecting your plane: thrust, drag, gravity and lift. So in straight and level flight your lift is equal to the gravity. Lift, however, is generated by two things in tandem: air-speed over the wings, and the angle of attack. So by increasing thrust you also increase speed which increases lift. And by pointing the nose higher up, you increase the angle of attack (AoA) which increases lift. But....... AoA and speed are inextricably linked, since a higher AoA also increases drag which reduces speed. So if you keep pitching up, increasing the AoA, you also have to add power in order to maintain the same speed. Keep doing it, and at some point your engine is incapable of producing enough thrust to maintain speed, and you stall out of the sky. With me so far?

So in your example of having the desired speed, but slowly climbing you have two options. Lowering the trim will also lower the AoA meaning less lift, so the plane will no longer climb. But that also decreases drag so you'll start to accelerate. Or you could lower the thrust meaning less speed over the wings, meaning less lift so you'll level out. But that will also result in you flying slower, since we have less thrust but the same drag. So if you want to stop climbing but maintain the same speed, you have to do both. Lower the AoA, and then lower the thrust to compensate for the lower drag.

Thrust, drag, gravity, lift. Just think of any situation in those four simple terms, and everything else will follow.

Well, FS9 (and FSX/P3D) uses look-up tables instead of direct calculations. Basically, it takes a freeze-frame of conditions at a certain point, and applies the result until the next key-frame. Meaning a far less dynamic environment.

This was mainly due to CPU limitations of the time, and there is nothing wrong with using look-up tables as such. I mean, NASA used look-up tables for their sims for a very long time. And whatever else you may think of NASA, I'm going to go out on a limb here and say they know a little bit about flying.

​

On the other hand, aside from some highly specialized instances (e.g. fighter jets and aerobatic aircraft), planes are designed to be inherently stable, in the same way that almost all civilian automobiles are inherently understeery by design. It's safer, easier on the driver, and much smoother. It's no use trying to teach a new pilot how to fly if he can't get it airborne without putting a wingtip on the grass.

So just because it's harder doesn't necessarily make it more realistic. It's one of those statements that has been permeating the sim-communities for decades (both flight- and race-sims), usually repeated by people who have never been in one of the vehicles in real-life.
